summary: Spanning Tree Protocol lets a switched network have redundant links without forwarding loops. Switches elect a root, compute loop-free paths toward it, and block the redundant ports.

sections.heading: The problem: Layer 2 loops
sections.body: Ethernet frames have no TTL. With redundant links, a broadcast can circulate forever and multiply (a broadcast storm), while MAC tables flap as the same source appears on multiple ports. STP prevents this by blocking some ports.

sections.heading: Root bridge election
sections.body: Every switch has a Bridge ID: a 16-bit priority (default 32768, in steps of 4096) followed by its MAC address. The switch with the lowest Bridge ID becomes the root. Switches exchange BPDUs (every 2 seconds) announcing the root they believe in.

sections.heading: Port roles
bullets: Root port: each non-root switch's single best path toward the root (lowest cumulative cost, then lowest sender ID).
Designated port: on each segment, the port that offers the best path to the root; it forwards.
Blocked/alternate port: everything else; receives BPDUs but forwards no data.

sections.heading: Path cost
sections.body: Costs are summed along the path to the root. Typical IEEE short-method values: 10 Mb/s = 100, 100 Mb/s = 19, 1 Gb/s = 4, 10 Gb/s = 2. Lower total cost wins; ties are broken by sender bridge ID and port ID.

sections.heading: Port states in classic STP
bullets: Blocking: discards data, listens to BPDUs.
Listening: transitions, no learning yet (forward delay 15 s).
Learning: builds the MAC table, still no forwarding (15 s).
Default timers: hello 2 s, forward delay 15 s, max age 20 s, so convergence takes 30-50 seconds.

sections.body: RSTP collapses states into discarding, learning, and forwarding and adds a proposal/agreement handshake so point-to-point links can move to forwarding in a second or less. It adds alternate and backup port roles that are ready to take over immediately.
Ports to end hosts should skip the delay (PortFast / edge port). BPDU Guard shuts such a port down if it ever receives a BPDU, preventing someone from attaching a switch and changing the topology.
PVST+ (Cisco) runs one tree per VLAN, enabling load balancing by choosing a different root per VLAN. MSTP (802.1s) maps groups of VLANs to a few instances, scaling better.

Root Guard stops a port from accepting a superior BPDU that would move the root. Loop Guard prevents a port from becoming designated if BPDUs stop arriving. Set priorities deliberately so the root is a core switch, not an arbitrary old one.
`show spanning-tree` lists the root, port roles, and states per VLAN; unexpected root bridges and flapping topology-change counters point to problems.
sections.code:
Switch# show spanning-tree vlan 10
  Root ID  Priority 24586  Address 0011.2233.4455
  Gi0/1  Root FWD 4  128.1  P2p

takeaways: STP elects the lowest Bridge ID as root, then keeps only the best loop-free paths.
Roles: root, designated, blocked; costs sum toward the root.
Classic STP converges in 30-50 s; RSTP in about a second.
Use PortFast + BPDU Guard on edge ports and set the root deliberately.
